title: The lion and the mouse
hookLine: a spared mouse later gnaws the lion free from a net (Aesop)

lines: A MOUSE ON A LION'S FACE.
cards: A flat tire on the highway. A night in the hospital. A week when everything falls apart.
The help that shows up in a pinch is often not who anyone would have guessed. Not the important friend, not the boss, not the one with the big job. The neighbor you barely knew.
The quiet coworker. The stranger. Aesop has a fable about exactly that, and it starts with a lion asleep in the sun.
A little mouse, running about, doesn't look where it's going, and runs right across the lion's face. The lion wakes up, and his huge paw comes down.

teach.h: SPARE ME, AND I'LL REPAY YOU.
teach.b: The mouse is pinned, about to be eaten. And it begs: please, let me go. Spare me, and one day I'll repay you.

teach.h: THE LION LAUGHS, AND LETS GO.

teach.b: A mouse, repay a lion? But he's amused, and not very hungry, so he lifts his paw, and the mouse runs off. Some time later, the lion is hunting in the forest and walks straight into a trap: a hunters' net.
The ropes close around him, and the more he struggles, the tighter it holds. He roars, and the whole forest hears it. So does the mouse.
It runs to the net, looks it over, and starts to gnaw. One rope. Then another.
Its teeth are tiny, but they're sharp, and it doesn't stop until there's a hole big enough, and the lion walks out free. And the mouse says, more or less: you laughed at me when I said I'd repay you.
Now you know even a mouse can help a lion. Two things are going on. First, the obvious one: don't judge who can help you by their size.
Small friends matter. Second, look at the lion's kindness. He didn't spare the mouse as an investment.
He laughed at the very idea of being repaid.
He let it go for nothing, and that's exactly the kind of kindness that comes back in ways nobody could plan.
You can't know which small, unrepayable kindness will turn out to be a rope someone gnaws through for you one day. So here's one way to carry it: be kind to the small ones anyway.

how: The lion and the mouse is still told to children as a lesson that even the small can help the strong.

o: a kindness given with no thought of return
a kindness you expect to be paid back for
a debt you owe that was never settled

games.q: what's inside the fable — tap the pairs.
p: spare me, and I'll repay you
the tighter he struggled, the tighter

s: the lion spared the mouse expecting a favor back
he laughed at the very idea that a mouse could repay a lion.

games.q: you're the lion. a tiny mouse under your paw begs to be let go, promising to repay you someday. what do you do?
o: eat it; a mouse can't repay a lion.
games.why: he laughs and lifts his paw. later, caught in a hunters' net, he's freed by that same mouse.

practice: Think of the people around you whose help you've never counted on: the kid next door, the person who cleans the office, the new member of the group, someone older, or younger, or quieter.
Pick one, and think of one small kindness you could offer them with no thought of getting anything back. Like the lion, just lift the paw.

wordCard.voice: unrepayable kindness. A lion spared a mouse, laughing at the very idea of repayment, and the mouse gnawed him free from a hunter's net anyway.
